articles.excerpt: A record from Rhodes about the stoixeia known as 'Anarathes' that dwell in ruins, trees, and rivers, and the 'lafrostoixeiotoi' — people who claim to have seen them.

content.value: They are afraid to come home late at night — "so as not to be caught by night", as they say — for fear of being seized by those "from outside here", the "Anarathes", the stoixeia. They believe that there are "haunted houses" (especially the ruins, called "chalatani"), as well as places, trees, and rivers where stoixeia dwell. There are many accounts of encounters with stoixeia.
There are people who tell of having seen them, and they are called "lafrostoixeiotoi" — those lightly touched by the spirits.

articles.title: Definition & Study of the Term 'Stoicheio' — Politis
articles.author: Nikolaos Politis
articles.excerpt: Folkloric definition and analysis of the term 'stoicheio' with etymological observations and cultural dimensions.

content.value: Stoicheia are souls of slain humans or animals, which attach themselves through spilled blood to a specific place, building, tree, ship, or even engraved coins, and through these transform into animate beings. This is not explicitly stated in folk tradition but is inferred from many testimonies.

Through the supernatural powers possessed by souls that have lost their bodies, stoicheia appear in the form of a human, animal, or other creature, capable of transforming at will. They also possess superhuman strength and can harm or benefit people in many ways. Their purpose is to guard and protect the place to which they have attached, to be beneficent to those who love them or are bound to them, and to be terrible and dangerous to those who try to harm them.

Stoicheia are especially dangerous to those who insult them, and only through magical techniques can humans neutralize them. When stoicheia grow angry or suffer, they abandon their stronghold, which then falls into ruin and decay — as if an animal has lost its soul.

Stoicheia differ from vrykolakes in two fundamental ways: vrykolakes are souls that have not separated from their body after death and are always malevolent, while stoicheia are souls that have attached to another body and are generally benevolent toward people.

Another category of stoicheia, distinct from the common type, are the stoicheia of the sea and lakes, which manifest primarily through the taste of a dish or drink that grants supernatural powers, and through entry into the liquid element.
Notes

Synonyms for 'stoicheio' include: zoudio, iskios, zouzolo, zoumpero, Therio. However, these words have a broader use and may refer to other demonic entities, while 'stoicheio' has primarily the meaning described above.

There are also more specific words used in different regions to denote particular kinds of stoicheia, such as: the house-snake (spitofidon), mnoioma, topakos, pergalio, Arapis, etc. The word 'stoicheio' originates among Greeks and other peoples of the Greek peninsula. For example, Albanians call it 'stixioya' or 'stixigya', Bulgarians call it 'stixigya', and Vlachs call it 'aiaxio' or 'diaxio' when referring to a stoicheio inhabiting a structure or house.

The word 'stoicheio' is pan-Hellenic; in the Rinassos region of Cappadocia it appears in the masculine gender, while among the Pontic Greeks it may transform into 'askestios' or 'skoistios', depending on local dialect.

As to its meaning, 'stoicheio' can also denote the soul that wanders after leaving the body during the first three nights, appearing as a white wisp of cloud or a small ball of cotton if the deceased was virtuous, or as a dark wisp if they were sinful.

Metaphorically, the word is used to describe something 'alone' or 'solitary', as in the expression 'einai stoicheio monaxo' ('it is a solitary stoicheio'), or in the folk song line 'but he had oxen of stoicheia, and iron ploughs'. In Kefalonia, the term 'psilo stoicheio' ('tall stoicheio') describes a person of great stature.

The phrase 'stoicheio tou spitiou' (the house's stoicheio) refers to a permanent resident of a house. The expression 'I have two stoicheia in the house' refers to two unmarried daughters or sisters who remain in the house for a long time without marrying.

The verb 'stoichiono' (derived from 'stoicheio') means to create a stoicheio through sacrifice — either of an animal (e.g. a rooster or other creature) rather than a human victim. This process relates to the cornerstone in construction, the first foundation of a building.

Metaphorically, 'stoichiono' means to pollute or defile a structure or space through murder, or more generally through any criminal act. The term 'stoicheiomenos' ('haunted house' or 'haunted place') refers to a place where a killing has occurred, because the place has been 'filled' with the victim's shed blood and 'haunted' by the act.

In the Pontic dialect, 'apostecheiomenos' or 'apestecheiomenos' describes someone in a state of terror or bewilderment, almost as if they have been 'passed through' by the influence of a stoicheio — suggesting an emotional or mental collapse as a result of spiritual contact.
The word 'stoicheion' appears to have passed through various stages of meaning and to have influenced different cultural and linguistic fields, as evidenced by its contemporary popular usage.

articles.title: Categories of Stoicheia
articles.excerpt: Analysis of the categories of stoicheia according to folkloric traditions: protective spirits, victims of injustice, heroes, and prophetic stoicheia.

content.value: Category — Guardian Spirits (Good Fortune)

The second category of stoicheia concerns those associated with monuments or objects intended to protect against hostile or malevolent forces. These monuments or objects are used to repel attacks, either from nearby areas or from larger regions such as entire cities. This category includes many types of ritual practices and objects.

Some examples include stoicheia connected to the protection of cities or regions, such as rituals or objects used for their safety. These stoicheia may involve special rituals that create a 'stoicheio' for the purpose of protecting or guarding an area. They also include stoicheia related to guarding storehouses, treasures, or other valuable resources, as well as those used to stabilize structures such as buildings and bridges.

A specific type of stoicheio concerns rituals connected with the stability and safety of buildings and other structures, achieved through the 'creation' of a stoicheio for each building — usually through ritual sacrificial means, such as the use of human or animal blood.

There are also rituals related to rivers, aimed at preventing flooding or other disasters they cause. All such rituals may be embedded in various folk legends and traditions concerning the protection of settlements or regions through special objects — such as statues or other works of art believed to contain the stoicheio that guards the area.

Modern traditions, drawing on these ancient practices, reflect the popular belief that statues or other artistic works contain the stoicheio that protects the space. This type of belief and practice appears to have survived in various folk myths and traditions.
Category — Victims of Injustice (Adikoχaménoi)

The third category of stoicheia concerns those connected with the haunting or presence of spirits or demons in places where human blood has been unjustly shed. In these cases, the spirits or demons are associated with places where crimes or injustices — such as murders — have occurred, and their presence is often linked to a need for restoration or revenge.

According to Byzantine traditions, these spirits or demons often appear in areas where crimes have occurred, and their presence is regarded as a kind of curse or misfortune for that place. This belief is bound up with the concept of moral injustice and the need for atonement or restoration.

This belief is expressed in legends and traditions in which spirits attack or appear to haunt the places where injustices — primarily murders or other forms of wrongdoing — have been committed. In traditional thought, this presence is linked to the idea that the blood of innocent people, when unjustly shed, invokes or manifests these stoicheia, which seek either to punish or to bring a form of purification for the injustice committed.
Category — Heroes

The fourth category of stoicheia refers to those connected with the lives of distinguished men — typically heroes or other important figures. These stoicheia are usually placed within columns or sculptural works of art, and their function is to protect the men for whom they were created, safeguarding their lives.

When the column or artwork is destroyed or collapses, the stoicheio is believed to be destroyed as well — and with it the life of the person to whom it is bound. In this sense, the stoicheio functions as a kind of protection for the prominent individual, and its destruction mirrors the destruction of his life.

This belief usually has mythical or religious roots, as these stoicheia were seen as a means of preserving the life and prosperity of great men, or as something connected to divine or heroic protection.
Category 5 — Prophetic Stoicheia

The final category refers to stoicheia connected with future events, carrying within them the story of what is to come. According to tradition, these stoicheia are often linked to prophecies or symbols that warn of approaching hardships, dangers, and calamities.

articles.title: Shadows — Iskioi
articles.excerpt: Etymological and folkloric analysis of the term 'iskios' and the related concepts of shadow and demonic influence.

content.value: The word 'derion' (therion — beast) is sometimes used to refer to the stoicheio, especially when speaking of a river, and carries a connection to the elements of nature — such as rivers or animals — which were considered manifestations of supernatural forces.

The use of the term 'iskios' is more widespread, as it has a broader meaning encompassing 'darkness' or 'shadow'. The word 'iskios' is connected to the ancient concept of the shadow and to references of the nocturnal realm. In folk belief it often represents something negative or threatening.

Furthermore, the verb 'iskionoame' derives from 'iskios' and carries the meaning of suffering some effect from the darkness or the shadow-spirit — essentially: 'I am afflicted by a demonic influence'.
This concept of the 'shadow' and its effect on humans is deeply rooted in ancient Greek thought, as the shadow was seen as connected to the mysteries of nature and the world of spirits.

The word 'iskios' (shadowy) is used to denote the shadow or darkness, and also refers to something that causes negative or demonic influence. It is sometimes used as a synonym for 'stoicheio', especially in northern Greek dialects.

The word 'iskios' refers to a phenomenon with two core meanings: on the one hand, it denotes the shadow or nocturnal apparition, and on the other, it signifies the negative influence caused by the presence of a spirit or demonic entity.
The word 'iskios' can also refer to a disease caused by demonic influence — such as a disease of goats. It is also used to describe the appearance of a person, i.e., their shadow or likeness.

The verb 'skiazo' originally means to cast a shadow, but is also used in the sense of 'to frighten' — to cause fear or anxiety. Thus the shadow can also carry a negative meaning, conveying threat or danger.
Nikolaos Politis — Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, Traditions Part B, 1904, p. 1065

articles.title: Kalymnos — Spirit of the Spring and Ritual Impurity
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Kalymnos about what happens to a person who dares approach the spirit's spring and drink from it while in a state of ritual impurity.

content.value: Kalymnos
A tradition of the Kalymnians (recorded by Yannis I. Zervos) tells what happens to someone who dares approach the spirit's spring and drink from its water while in an impure state:

"The Ratselaris Chouridas, who was then around forty years old, told me the following story: 'One midday, my mother-in-law, my sister-in-law, and I were walking together, and as we were approaching the spring, my aunt — who was in an impure state — drank from the water. Immediately her face contorted, and she began trembling uncontrollably.'"

"The Sakelaris Chouridas, who was around forty years old, told me the following story: 'One midday, we were coming from Vathy together with my mother-in-law and my sister-in-law. As we were climbing the hill, my sister-in-law — who was in an impure state — drank from the spring. At once her face twisted and she fell into terrible convulsions.'"
Nikolaos Politis — Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, Traditions Part B, 1904, p. 1072

articles.title: Pergalio — Zakynthos
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Zakynthos about the house-spirit known as 'Pergalio', with its Latin etymology and connection to the foundations of a home.

content.value: 'Pergalio' is the name used only in Zakynthos for the spirit of the house. The word derives from the Latin 'rosetum' (Italian 'roseto', Romanian 'roseț'), meaning 'shrub'. Other forms of the word — 'pergoulo', 'pergoulia', 'perroglia' — are widely used in various parts of Greece to refer to a vine trellis. How the word came to denote the house-spirit is unclear and difficult to determine.
The tradition explicitly states that the 'Pergalio' is the person whose shadow was buried beneath the foundations of the house.
Nikolaos Politis — Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, Traditions Part B, 1904, p. 1100

articles.title: Perganta — Definition and Meaning
articles.excerpt: A note on the metaphorical use of the term 'Perganta' for a demon of industriousness and its connection to nautical terminology.

content.value: According to G. Kremon (in the Athenian newspaper 'Nea Ellas', no. 56, 2 November 1874):

B. Schmidt (Volksleben, p. 142) records the enigmatic expression 'Perganta', used to denote a hardworking and industrious woman. The name of this patron daemon of textile work (the processing of wool or fibres) has been transferred from the common word 'perganti', found in many parts of Greece, meaning a multi-oared fast vessel. This metaphorical transfer of names reflects the tendency to associate human or divine characteristics with specific objects or situations — a common feature of Greek tradition and culture.
With this reference, Kremon highlights the metaphorical use of names tied to everyday life and the practices of the era, used to denote characters or forces — whether positive or negative.
For a literary adaptation of such traditions see: Parnassos, vol. 7, p. 691 ff. (Passagiannis, 'The Wretched House').
Nikolaos Politis — Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, Traditions Part B, 1904, p. 1102

articles.title: The Stoicheio and Haunted Houses
articles.excerpt: A distinction between the protective house-spirit (stoicheio) and the malevolent demons of haunted houses in Greek folk belief.

content.value: The belief in haunted houses differs from the belief in the house-stoicheio. The house-stoicheio, as noted earlier, is the soul that attaches to the building, guarding and protecting its residents and generally showing goodwill toward them. A house that possesses such a stoicheio is not considered dangerous and is not called 'haunted'. By contrast, haunted houses may harbour malevolent demons that cause fear, destruction, and dangerous situations.

These stoicheia appear either in various forms or as invisible spirits, creating noises, disorder, and confusion — striking or terrorizing those who dare to spend the night in a house where these phantoms dwell. Such spirits may also cause madness, or bring incurable diseases and other misfortunes.

Many traditions exist about haunted houses beyond those mentioned here. As evidenced by other records, this belief has deep roots in Greek folklore, as shown also by articles in Athenian newspapers from 1898.
Nikolaos Politis — Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, Traditions Part B, 1904, p. 1103

articles.title: The Cursed House of Kyparissia
articles.excerpt: An account of a cursed house in Kyparissia where successive families suffered tragedies — recorded in the newspaper 'Kairoi', 1893.

content.value: A report from Kyparissia states the following: There exist superstitions and beliefs that are fostered either by bad luck, by coincidences, or by circumstances. In Kyparissia there are houses about which it is believed that every tenant will suffer some misfortune. Among these is the house of the Tourkolia heirs. In this recently built house, the first occupant — a steward — died within a few months. The next tenant lost his wife and one of his children within eight days.

A third tenant followed, and he lost all his children. In the end, none of the residents of this house escaped family tragedy. The second-to-last occupant was myself — I lost my first child and was forced to vacate before my lease ended. The last tenant is the pharmacist Mr Io. Despotopoulos, who still lives there. And he too, that unfortunate man — his only son, a twelve-year-old boy, once attempted suicide, and was recently wounded by a firearm held by another child who was being careless, as they say. All this happened just four months ago, in that house.
Because of the misfortunes that befall its occupants, this house is called haunted, cursed, unlucky, terrible, and dreadful.
Nikolaos Politis — Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, Traditions Part B, 1904, p. 1104

articles.title: Battle of the Stoicheia — Gkioza, Feneos, Corinthia
articles.excerpt: A tradition about battles between village, church, and nature stoicheia in Gkioza, Feneos — their forms, tactics, and the fate of villagers when their spirit is defeated.

content.value: Gkioza, Feneos, Corinthia

"From G. Velmachos, Priest (1896): 'Just as every house and every church has its own stoicheio, so too does every village have its own stoicheio. The life and prosperity of the villagers are inseparably bound to the existence of the village stoicheio, and if it is harmed or defeated in battle, the villagers suffer misfortune — their crops fail, livestock die, and calamities befall them.'"

"Very often the stoicheio of one village battles the stoicheio of a neighbouring village, just as the stoicheia of different churches within the same village fight each other, as do the stoicheia of mountains, lakes, waters, the sea, and trees. In their battles, stoicheia appear in various forms — as animals, humans, winds, or fire."

"The stronger or more dangerous stoicheia fight their opponents by hurling quantities of milk, or by throwing balls of tallow, or by summoning the help of a human who shoots the enemy stoicheio with his left hand, or strikes it with a club, or pelts it with tallow-balls."

articles.title: Kalymnos — Candle at the Spirit's Fountain
articles.excerpt: A traditional practice of lighting a candle in honour of the stoicheio of a particular fountain in Kalymnos, as recalled by a local.

content.value: In Kalymnos, according to Mr Yannis K. Zervos, the inhabitants used to light a candle in honour of the stoicheio of a particular fountain. He recalls:

"We were sitting with Stavris the shepherd (it must have been around the same period) under the pomegranate tree near the fountain at the Skalia. As I looked at the fountain with its old arch, I remembered that my grandfather used to send me many times to light the candle that hung in the middle of the arch."
This practice was part of the local tradition to ensure good fortune and protection from evil spirits.

articles.excerpt: A first-hand account of a man pursued by a stoicheio at the Kakes Petres area of Samos — a crimson beast that chased him until he found sanctuary in a chapel.

content.value: A man who had been pursued by a stoicheio recounted, still with terror in his heart, that some years earlier, while staying at the place called 'Kakes Petres' in the Karlovasioi district, he saw five or six young partridges emerge from a bush. He ran after the birds and chased them, and they led him away until he was far from the path.

Then, from another bush, a strange creature emerged — bright crimson and resembling a pig. The man fled at a run, but the creature began to pursue him. He could hear its heavy footsteps behind him as he ran, and the wretched man was saved only by ducking into a small chapel that he found in his path.

articles.title: The Apex of the Katevátos — Legend of Arachova
articles.excerpt: A traditional tale about the mythical spirit Katevátos and the battle of the elements on the peaks of Liákoura above Arachova.

content.value: The Katevátos is an old man with white hair and a fierce appearance. In winter he battles the other stoicheia on the peaks of Liákoura. When the elements clash, the mountain trembles, groans, and is buried in snow, unable to bear the rage of the demons. The Katevátos descends, the wind howls, and the snow covers everything. This is the 'apogee' — the climax of the battle.

About a hundred years ago, the monk Gerótheos of the Monastery of Hosios Loukas sought to witness with his own eyes the battle of the spirits and the fearful apogee. Provisioned for the journey, he climbed Liákoura in November and took shelter in a cave near the summit — and there he waited for the battle to begin.

articles.title: The Anaskelades — Crete
articles.excerpt: A folk account of the demonic donkeys called 'anaskelades' and the protective practices used against them on nocturnal roads in Crete.

content.value: Many times, when someone walks the road at night, they come across a donkey grazing at the side of the path. If they want to ride it for a rest, the donkey stands quietly and lets them mount.

But before long it starts to grow taller and wilder, rising above the trees and the ravines. The rider feels as if they have been carried away from their world. Then they begin to cross themselves and call upon the Virgin Mary — and suddenly they find themselves back where they started, with the donkey gone.
The donkey then vanishes before them, but fills the whole place with fire and smoke from its flatulence. These donkeys, in our region, are called 'anaskelades'.

To be certain that a donkey found at night is not an anaskelás, before mounting it one must grab it by the tail and say a specific protective phrase. If it is an anaskelás, it will flee amid fire and smoke and will not be seen again.

But if one forgets and mounts without the phrase, the creature may suddenly place a pentagram on their head — and from that moment they cannot easily escape; they are carried wherever it wills, as if cursed.

articles.title: Haunted Trees — Kozani
articles.excerpt: Folk practices from Kozani for dealing with tree-spirits and avoiding their wrath when felling ancient and solitary trees.

content.value: Large and ancient trees are haunted, and people avoid sitting long beneath them or sleeping in their shade, lest they suffer harm.

When woodcutters fell such a tree and see it beginning to topple, they throw themselves face-down on the ground and make no sound — so that the soul of the tree will not sense their presence as it departs and, in its anger, strike them.

And into the trunk, at the moment of cutting, they wedge a stone to stop the soul of the tree from rushing out violently — for otherwise it would harm them and split them in two at the waist, bringing severe back pains.

articles.title: The Haunted Branch — Trikala
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Trikala about haunted trees and the fate of those who plant them — the story of Petros and the walnut tree that made him gravely ill.

content.value: Many large and solitary trees are haunted, each guarded by its own stoicheio — which is why no one dares disturb them. A haunted tree is easily recognized because it grows unnaturally fast and becomes very strong. Whoever plants such a tree takes on its spirit, and as the tree grows, so their own body prospers; but when the tree is cut, the person wastes away and may die.
About fifty years ago, Petros, the son of Papagiannis in Trikala, planted a walnut tree when he was a small boy in his father's garden. The tree grew very quickly — but Petros fell gravely ill.
His father, Papagiannis, immediately had the walnut tree cut down so that the stoicheio would not suffocate his son — and the boy recovered.

articles.title: Lost Things — Zakynthos
articles.excerpt: A folk account from Zakynthos about mysterious disappearances of objects and the role of the house-spirit, which keeps what falls and grows angry if complained about.

content.value: In a certain house, whatever fell to the floor went missing — coins, jewellery, buttons, needles. The housewife never complained. The house ran as God willed.

One day a friend forgot her ring, which she had been showing on the sofa. When she left, it was spotted and placed on the dresser; the housewife called her child to take it to her. The child came, took the ring — and it fell from his hand to the floor. They looked, but it was nowhere to be found.
The husband came in the meantime and the child said where the ring had fallen. They searched everywhere — nothing. Then the woman confessed to her husband that whatever fell in the house disappeared.
What could be done? The husband believed it. He beat his wife, and went out and bought a replacement ring for the guest. From that moment on, fire broke into the house — misfortunes upon misfortunes.
A wise woman who heard of it told them to leave at once, for the spirit of the house was angry with them because they had complained about the disappearances.

When something falls and cannot be found, it is taken by the house spirit, which keeps it and gives back its value many times over in another form. But when complaints are made, the spirit grows angry — and if they do not leave the house, misfortunes follow.

articles.title: The Haunted House — Samos
articles.excerpt: An account of a haunted house in Samos: unseen footsteps, a presence that shared a bed, and the fate of those who dared to stay the night.

content.value: Many houses are haunted, and no one dares to stay in them at night. Many of those who happened to stay there found their bodies darkened with bruises and swollen.

A literate man was sitting in his room one night writing when he suddenly heard someone ascending the staircase — though the front door was closed. He rose in puzzlement to see who was there, when his own room door — which was also locked — swung open by itself. He was petrified with fear and ran quietly and hid himself in his bed.
But before long he felt the sheets stir and sensed that something had come and lain down in the same bed, pressing closer and closer to him until the man nearly burst from terror.
Everyone sleeping in the house ran to see what had happened to him, and he told them — but the stoicheio had vanished.

articles.title: The Moros of the Well — Zakynthos
articles.excerpt: A folk tale from Zakynthos about a handsome young man who appeared daily at a well, and whose jealous temper led to a death.

content.value: A young woman went to the well every midday to fetch water. There, at the parapet, a young Moorish-looking man with a pipe and a small fez was always waiting — handsome, with two large blue eyes. Whenever he saw her, he would take her bucket, fill it, and bring it to her.

In time the girl became a bride. Her new husband, who had heard about this, told her never to go back for water from that well. But she wanted to go — she had it in her mind that the young man might show her where some treasure was buried.

One midday the husband saw that his bride was heading toward the well and followed her. When she arrived he said: 'Did I not tell you not to come back?' And while he continued to scold her, he vanished.
A moment later voices were heard coming from inside the well. The spirit had thrown him in. The girl was terrified and never went back to the well.
That night she saw him in a dream. She woke at dawn, left for town, and never returned to the village out of fear.

articles.title: The Tentzerakis — Oichalia, Messenia
articles.excerpt: A dramatic first-hand account from Oichalia, Messenia: an encounter with the stoicheio known as Tentzerakis — a fearsome creature that appears with a great pot on its head.

content.value: Kalimpaki is a haunted place, between Dousila and Tryfa in the municipality of Andania. A stoicheio appears there that the people call 'Tentzerakis', because it shows itself with a great cauldron on its head.

"We set out one day to go to Tryfa, to my brother-in-law Nikolos Kontaxis — it had been a while since we'd gone that way, and we wanted nothing to 'stick' to us on the road. We found Nikolos, sat down, he treated us well, and we talked for a while."

"One night there was a bright moon like daylight, and he was grazing his sheep around Kalimpaki. He stretched out on a bramble patch and seemed to doze off. Then he heard: bra, bra, bra. He looked — and saw an enormous creature with enormous paws, and a great cauldron on its head."
"'All right,' says Nikolos, 'for good or ill let us go around the threshing floor.' I said to him: 'No.' He said: 'You go that way and I'll go this way — and if you hear a shout, come running.'"

"We set off — I through the threshing floors and he through Kalimpaki. Barely had he gone a step when — bang! 'Haha,' I said to myself, 'Tassis got what was coming to him.' I ran up in front. 'Hey Tassis,' I shouted, 'what happened to you?' I saw him gasping. He collapsed to the ground."

articles.title: The Haunted Bridge — Tyrnavos
articles.excerpt: A legend from Tyrnavos about the single-arched bridge of Salamvrias, which had to be consecrated with a human sacrifice before it would stand — and has trembled and wept ever since.

content.value: The single-arched bridge of Salamvrias, near the village of Mousoulár in the municipality of Tyrnavos, is haunted. As the song says, when it was being built, it fell apart every night.

They consecrated sheep — it would not hold. They consecrated a poor child — still it leaned to one side. Until finally they consecrated the head mason's wife. And she cursed it: to tremble as her heart trembled, and to make all who passed over it weep.
And now the bridge tilts first to the right, then to the left — and every stranger who crosses it is overcome by weeping, for before they cross, some sudden misfortune always finds them.

articles.title: The Stoicheio of the Young Hero — Lampeia, Elis
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Lampeia, Elis about a battle between stoicheia — and the clever tactic of the victorious spirit that used a hidden man with an iron club.

content.value: While the stoicheia were fighting each other — appearing as grey horses and dark horses — the current stoicheio won and drove away the other by this device:

It first dug the earth with its hoof, made a pit, hid a man inside it, gave him an iron club, and commanded him to strike the opposing stoicheio on the left elbow-root. And in this way it defeated and drove it off.

During the battle, however, the hidden man once accidentally struck his own allies. They then called out the signal: 'Kommos in your hands!' — and the man understood his mistake and did not strike his allies again.

articles.title: The Chiliantrissa of Symi
articles.excerpt: A tradition from Symi about the terrifying stoicheio known as the Chiliantrissa — appearing as a great sow followed by thousands of piglets — which haunted the Castle until a holy procession drove it away.

content.value: The Chiliantrissa was the most fearsome stoicheio: it appeared as a whole sow (gourouna), followed by thousands of little piglets (gourounakia). It dwelt in the Castle and emerged from the iron gate at midnight, on moonless nights, running along all the roads.
The little piglets that followed ran with it and squealed, causing great uproar — and all who heard it shuddered and trembled. It vanished when the cock crowed.

They say it ceased to appear from the time that a litany was performed with the holy icons from the church of the Panagia of the Castle, through all the roads it used to travel. Since then it only appears very rarely.

Thus, one man who once found himself at midnight in an open area in the parish of Agia Triada saw a flock of goats — something unusual in that location. While he was wondering how they got there and whose they were, he suddenly felt himself pushed aside by something invisible. As he continued walking, he reached a vaulted passage and stretched out his hand — he grasped someone, then lost them. He reached home barely alive — the encounter had shaken him deeply.

articles.title: The Beast of Agoriani or the Stoicheio of the Marsh — Phocis
articles.excerpt: An account from Phocis of a marsh-dwelling spirit that terrified local villagers with its wailing — believed to have appeared when the swamp was being drained. It was never heard again after drainage was complete.

content.value: An excursion to the municipality of Dorieon in Phocis is described. On an Easter Day some years prior, terror had gripped the inhabitants of the area after word spread that between Agoriani and Souvala, in a well-known swamp called 'Valtos', a monstrous creature had appeared, crying out with a terrible voice in the night.

The event had thrown the villagers into upheaval. All described the beast with vivid detail — some said they saw it stirring the water and the aquatic trees of the marsh as it moved; others said it had an enormous wild-boar head with phosphorescent eyes.

That Easter, the inhabitants of Souvala were somber and joyless, without gunshots or songs, fearing that the people of Agoriani had been destroyed by the beast. They were reassured when they learned that the inhabitants of Kato Agoriani had taken precautions and sheltered indoors.

The appearance of the beast was attributed by many villagers — especially the elders — to the community of Agoriani's attempt to drain the swamp, and to the digging of large ditches to channel the stagnant waters into the nearby stream of Agia Eleousa.
In the end, the drainage proceeded — and after the waters were channelled away, the stoicheio was never heard again.

articles.title: The Tradition of the Stoicheia in Vourvoura, Arcadia
articles.excerpt: A detailed account of the stoicheia traditions of Vourvoura: house-spirits appearing as harmless snakes, village-spirits as dappled bulls, battles between village spirits, and elders who had spoken with them.

content.value: It is believed that inside every house there is a stoicheio that protects it — the guardian of the house, appearing in the form of a harmless snake. It is considered a great act of impiety to kill one's house-guardian.
And just as every house has its own guardian who watches over its inhabitants, so too does every village have its own stoicheio that protects the village — taking the form of a dappled bull.
Among the stoicheia of different villages, battles sometimes occur that last many hours.

In earlier times, word spread that the stoicheio of Vourvoura had fought the stoicheio of Kastri. The stoicheio of Vourvoura won — and from that moment the flow of the waters changed, so that instead of flowing toward Kastri they began flowing toward Vourvoura.
The village stoicheia were seen by the elders, and many had spoken with them.

articles.title: Friends with the Stoicheio of Vourvoura
articles.excerpt: A folk tale from Vourvoura about Voilas, who befriended the village stoicheio. After insulting its breath, the stoicheio made him bury an axe in its back — the wound healed, but the offence was never forgotten.

content.value: Voilas, an inhabitant of Vourvoura, was on friendly terms with the village stoicheio. He would go and greet it many times. One time when he went to greet it, he told it that it was good and worthy — but that its breath smelled like a dog.
The stoicheio did not answer, but picked up an axe and told Voilas to strike it as hard as he could in the back.
He hesitated, but the stoicheio urged him to do it.
Voilas raised the axe and struck it with all his strength — so hard that the entire axe buried itself in the stoicheio's back.
'Now go,' the stoicheio said — and Voilas left.
Out of fear, he took three years before he dared return to see the stoicheio. When he went back, the stoicheio welcomed him and asked why he had taken so long.
He hesitated to answer out of fear. The stoicheio told him to look at its back. Voilas looked and said happily that the wound had healed completely.
The stoicheio replied that the wound had healed completely — but what he had said to it had not passed, and never would.

articles.title: The Tradition of the Stoicheia in Trikala, Corinthia
articles.excerpt: A rich account of stoicheio beliefs in Trikala, Corinthia: their haunts, appearances, and the tale of two poor brothers — one of whom learned the language of frogs and used it to save himself from a stoicheio in a tower.

content.value: In Trikala and the surrounding area, there is a widespread belief that stoicheia have specific dwelling-places: in desolate spots, caves, ravines, gorges, uninhabited houses, and towers. They say: 'Keep away from that ravine.'
They also say that stoicheia emerge at night and vanish at dawn when the first cock crows. Stoicheia make sounds like animals, and sometimes cry like children.
The stoicheio at the place called 'Spilies' has been seen by many, sitting and smoking a cigarette.
Whoever sees a stoicheio and is carrying a weapon must shoot it immediately with the left hand — because if they shoot with the right hand it has no effect, and the arm withers.

In Trikala it is also believed that whoever plants in their garden an apple tree, walnut tree, or cherry tree, and a branch grows very large — if the person who planted it falls ill, they cut the branch completely so the sick person will not die, believing the fates of the tree and the planter are intertwined.
About the stoicheia of Trikala, the following tale is told:

Once, two poor brothers put bread in their satchels and set off into the world to find work. They walked and walked, and one midday sat down in the shade of a tree to eat. The elder brother fell asleep.
The elder woke and told him to rise and go seek work. The younger answered that he would not come — he would stay and learn the language of the frogs.
The elder continued on his way and one night arrived at a tower in a wilderness and went inside to sleep. He was asked who he was and answered.

They told him immediately to go upstairs because the lord of the tower was ill — he had stomach pains — and asked if he could cure him. 'I can and more than can,' he answered — not knowing the lord of the tower was a stoicheio.
To be cured, the stoicheio was advised to find a human being and eat him. The stoicheio immediately asked where it would find another human besides the man himself — and ate him.

The younger brother, who had by now mastered the language of the frogs, set out to find his elder brother. By chance he passed the same tower. He was asked the same questions as his brother and answered. Then the younger brother commanded the frog that lived inside the stoicheio to come out — and the stoicheio was healed.
He was saved from the stoicheio and rewarded most generously.

content.value: The wells of the village, generally, are haunted. It seems stoicheia are especially fond of them. By day they hide inside the well, only to emerge at night filled with malice toward people.
At the burial mounds outside the village — and sometimes inside it — many have happened to see fires in the evenings. It would not be amiss if someone could approach and dig.
At that spot there is buried treasure. But the approach is dangerous. Some phantom will leap from the fire in the form of a beast, fated to guard the treasure — and then woe to the bold intruder.
In daylight it is futile to dig, because the treasure disappears.
